chapter_theme: In the close of the last ilampakam the poem sets the court's lovemaking beside the ascetics' penance, which ends in death on a mountain and rebirth as gods in heavenly pleasure, then ends with the poet's praise of the three-umbrella Lord's feet and of the work's hearers.

cast.role: the lovers of the pleasure scene, women and men named only as groups
the youth Nandan, who with his companions takes up penance
the companions who share the penance
the ascetics reborn as gods who enjoy heaven's pleasure
the poet speaking in the first person at the end of the work

3122.reading: Men embrace the long-haired women as wishing-trees are wrapped in creepers of desire, and reach the pleasure that is the comfort of their breasts.
3122.nuance: The verse names no one; that these are the hero's household is carried from the ilampakam, not from the words. The simile of the heavenly wishing-tree already puts the bed in the language of paradise.
3122.event: The lovers of the court lie in each other's arms and take their pleasure.

3123.reading: The fruit of the pleasure of union is the lovers' quarrel; the wet-eyed glances of the golden-boughed women pierce the hearts of the men in their leaf-patterned jewels.
3123.nuance: Union and sulking are set as seed and fruit, so the quarrel is a part of the pleasure and not its break.
3123.event: The women sulk and their glances pierce the men's hearts.

3124.reading: The lily-eyed women cast reproachful side-glances while their anklets ring and the men's hair is stirred; the play of the lovers' quarrel goes on.
3124.nuance: The first two lines turn on a clause (பெண்பெயர் நிவிற்றினீர்) that I cannot parse with confidence; the reading rests on lines 3 and 4 only.
3124.event: The women reproach the men in play, with glances and sounding anklets.

3125.reading: A soft-footed, flower-browed woman fears that the flowers set in the man's hair have pained the lady's heart, and the verse calls such fear a fault of its own.
3125.nuance: Who is meant by 'the lady' and whose fault the last line names are not fixed by the words.
3125.event: A woman frets that she has hurt another's feelings with the flowers in a man's hair.

3126.reading: The lovers fasten the white anklet strings, praise the lily-eyed beauty and set a honeyed wreath on her, asking whether eyes that saw her could ever blink.
3126.nuance: The sentence is carried by three participles and ends in verse 3127, so the last line is read as an offering of the wreath; this is the less certain half.
3126.event: The men dress the women and praise their eyes.

3127.reading: The women, bright as lightning, put on girdles of many gems, settle them, brush pollen powder over their golden breasts, and their two gem earrings seem to laugh.
3127.event: The women adorn themselves after love.

3128.reading: The earrings of the dark-haired woman, shaking, seem to laugh so that all feel shame, as if saying that those who did the deed and those it was done to will each come to know everything.
3128.nuance: The saying ascribed to the earrings echoes a wording of deed and its object (செய்த, செயப்பட்டார்), which a reader may take as a faint hint at karma; the verse does not draw the doctrine out.
3128.event: The woman's earrings shake in laughter and shame those present.

3129.reading: The anklets sound, the jasmine garlands scatter, the worn wreaths roll about, and the girdles on the women's hips gape and gasp in the heat of love.
3129.event: The lovers' union breaks the women's ornaments.

3130.reading: The slender women take up, as if it were a drink named desire mixed with toddy, a gem cup and drink, trembling and wilting.
3130.nuance: Desire is given the name of the drink itself; the drink is a figure for the lovers' pleasure and is not a separate scene of drinking.
3130.event: The women drink from gem cups and tremble.

3131.reading: After the women of soft speech have drunk to the full the honeyed nectar of heat and lived on rejoicing, the narrator turns to tell what befell the righteous ascetics.
3131.nuance: The turn from the bed to the ascetics (செம்மை மாதவர்) is the hinge of the chapter: the poet gives no argument, he lays the two lives side by side.
3131.event: The narrator closes the scene of pleasure and turns to the ascetics.

3132.reading: Like the white moon on a full-moon day, the youth Nandan and his companions, while each day others tremble, pile up good penance by their own effort and gain themselves.
3132.nuance: That 'the youth' (காளை) is Civakan and not a second person cannot be told from the words; Nandan is named, and the group is read as ascetics only from the next verse.
3132.event: Nandan and his companions practise penance.

claims.claim: a man gains himself by the penance he piles up with his own effort

3133.reading: With meditation and fasting, which wash off evil deeds, and by reverence to the Teacher (தீர்த்தன்), the righteous move like bees on flowers and fear even the tongue's craving as they fear poison.
3133.nuance: தீர்த்தன் may be the Tirthankara or a bathing-place figure; the epic's Jain setting makes the first likelier.
3133.event: The ascetics fast and meditate and fear the craving of the tongue.

claims.claim: fasting joined to meditation washes off evil deeds
the craving of the tongue is to be feared as poison

3134.reading: When the time bound in the womb at conception came, the five of them ended their lives on a mountain that rises like a white crescent horn, and became gods, as splendid as the appearance of Tiru.
3134.nuance: The ascetics' penance here ends in heaven, not yet in release; the verses after it spend seven stanzas on heavenly pleasure, which is a reward that the Jain scheme counts below release.
3134.event: The five ascetics die on a mountain and are reborn as gods.

claims.claim: the span of a life is fixed at conception and ends when its time comes
penance ends in rebirth as a god

3135.reading: The gods who once burned in penance against the god of love now enjoy the dark-eyed, peacock-like women as bull elephants enjoy the herds of cow elephants.
3135.nuance: The first line is read as a reversal: those who fought desire through penance now live in it. The identification of the gods with the ascetics is from the sequence of verses, not from a word in this one.
3135.event: The new gods take their pleasure with the heavenly women.

3136.reading: The heavenly women's earrings, bows of brows and garlands tremble and fall, their girdles and anklets ring, and the breasts meet like armies on the field of love.
3136.nuance: The battle of the breasts is the same figure that verse 3140 pursues with a weapon of sulking.
3136.event: The gods and the women join in love-play, imagined as a battle.

3137.reading: Saffron paste rubs off the breasts and chests, a plough of eager love sows a harvest of endless enjoyment, and the immortals sink in the whirlpool of desire, two becoming many in their pleasure.
3137.nuance: The gods are said to be caught in a net of desire and a whirlpool, images that elsewhere in the work belong to bondage.
3137.event: The gods lose themselves in love.

3138.reading: To the beat of drums, the lute, the flute and the dance, the gods feast their eyes on the women and take joy in the garden of desire.
3138.event: The gods watch dance and music and are feasted by the women.

3139.reading: The women with flowers in their hair and pearls on their shoulders pierce the men's hearts with sidelong looks, and the men fall on their breasts, smearing the sandal paste.
3139.event: The gods are pierced by glances and fall on the women's breasts.

3140.reading: The women's spear-bright eyes, with the hand of love as messenger, join in the sulking-war, and by their play the heaven of the gods shines.
3140.nuance: Love is a war here in which sulking is the arms and the hand is the messenger, a figure that borrows the vocabulary of kings.
3140.event: The gods and women quarrel and make up in the play of love.

3141.reading: Drinking the honey of desire in the bodies of the slender-waisted women, the gods sink in a sea of senses beyond rival.
3141.nuance: The sinking (ஆழ்ந்தார்) is praise in the poet's mouth, but the sea of senses recalls the image of birth as a sea that the last verses name as a thing to cross.
3141.event: The gods drink their fill of pleasure and sink in the sea of sense.

claims.claim: the pleasures of the gods' world are a sea in which they sink, and they are without a rival

3142.reading: The poet compares the Arhat's feet, set upon a gem-studded pedestal bright as the Lord's own radiance, and places them on his head.
3142.nuance: முக்குடையான் is the Arhat, the three umbrellas being his sign in Jain worship; the rest is a long simile for his golden pedestal.
3142.event: The poet bows his head to the feet of the three-umbrella Lord.

claims.claim: the Arhat of the three umbrellas is to be worshipped at his feet

3143.reading: Those who read and understand the Cintamani, which is like the pearls a conch gave up from the sea strung into a fine rope, and those who hear it, will rise in this way, and the lotus goddess will guard them.
3143.nuance: The fruit named is worldly, since Tiru, the lotus goddess of fortune, guards the hearers; the epic's last ilampakam is called release, but its closing blessing is of prosperity.
3143.event: The poet states the fruit of reading and hearing his work.

claims.claim: those who learn and hear this work rise in the world and are guarded by Tiru

3144.reading: Having sung the feet of the Lord on whose chest the lotus goddess dwells, the poet says that he has scattered the story of the Cintamani, and that the wise gain an undying lamp and good gem.
3144.nuance: The Lord with Tiru on his chest is a figure the Vaishnava tradition also uses; here the three-umbrella Arhat is meant by the context of the closing verses, which is the less certain of two readings.
3144.event: The poet ends the telling of the story with praise of the Lord's feet.

claims.claim: the Lord's feet are to be praised, and those who understand the story gain an undying light

3145.reading: The poet, raising his hands, praises with the flowers of his words the feet of the three-umbrella Lord, a spotless moon that rises from the sea of deeds and breaks the dark of deeds' binding.
3145.nuance: The sea is of deeds (செய்வினை), not of births, so the work ends on the figure of karma as the water to be crossed, and gives its closing act to a hymn.
3145.event: The poet offers his poem as a flower at the Lord's feet and ends the work.

claims.claim: the Lord's feet free one from the sea of deeds and the darkness of karma

links.note: 3132 has Nandan and his friends piling up penance by effort; 3134 ends their lives on the mountain with rebirth as gods.
links.teaches: The penance begun in one verse comes to its fruit two verses later, so the story shows the deed ripening into a heavenly birth and not into release.

links.note: 3133 says fasting and meditation wash off evil deeds; 3145 closes on the Lord's feet as the way across the sea of deeds.
links.teaches: The first verse gives the ascetic's own washing of deeds, the last the worshipper's crossing by the Lord's feet, so the work ends by joining effort and devotion.

links.note: 3122 sets the lovers as wishing-trees wrapped in creepers; 3141 puts the gods in a sea of the senses, so one pleasure is drawn at two levels.
links.teaches: The poet writes human and heavenly love with the same figures, so the heaven reached by penance is a purer form of the bed that penance left.

links.note: 3133 says fasting and meditation wash off evil deeds; Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives off sin as a lamp drives off dark, but only while the good deeds last.
links.teaches: The story shows the ascetics' fast washing deeds away, and the quatrain adds that the lamp burns only while its oil of good deeds holds.

gains.a: the verse's washing of deeds acquires a limit, that austerity works only while the store of good deeds lasts, which is not said in the verse
gains.b: the quatrain's lamp and oil acquire a case in which a company of ascetics is seen to carry the austerity through to their deaths

links.note: 3134 has the penance end in birth as gods; Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of I and mine goes to a world above the gods.
links.teaches: The epic's ascetics end among the gods, but the couplet puts above the gods a world reached only by cutting off the self, so heaven is not the last goal.

gains.a: the rebirth among gods is shown as not the top of the scale, which the verse itself does not say
gains.b: the couplet's world above the gods is given a case of ascetics who stop at heaven short of it

links.note: 3145 ends on the Lord's feet as the way over the sea of deeds; Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births.
links.teaches: Both place the Lord's feet beyond a sea, but the Cintamani names the water as deeds and the Kural as births, so the epic fixes on karma as the thing to be crossed.

gains.a: the sea is placed in a fuller tradition of birth as the sea to be crossed, so karma and rebirth are read together
gains.b: the couplet's sea of births is given a cause by the epic, since the water is made of deeds

source_issues: Verses 3136 to 3138, 3142, 3143 and 3145 print in eight half-lines and were joined into four; the joins are the build's.
Verses 3142 to 3145 are the poet's closing praise and sit outside the story; the identification of the Lord in 3144 is from context, not from a naming word.
